0.title: Faith That Works: The Letter of James
0.overview:
James is the most practical book in the New Testament — and one of the most misunderstood. Martin Luther famously called it “an epistle of straw,” contrasting its apparent emphasis on works with Paul’s gospel of grace. He was wrong — his polemical situation against Roman Catholic merit theology made him over-read James as a rival to Paul rather than as his complement. Read on its own terms, James is not a rival to the gospel of grace but its most searching ethical application: what does genuine, living, gospel-produced faith actually look like? The answer is not passive and invisible. It looks like patience in trials, generosity to the poor, a bridled tongue, peaceful wisdom, and prayer that moves heaven.

The author identifies himself as “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). The most natural identification is James the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church, the man who had not believed in Jesus during his earthly ministry (John 7:5) but was transformed by a resurrection appearance (1 Cor 15:7) into the pillar of the first church (Gal 2:9) and its martyred leader (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9). The letter was probably written before the Jerusalem Council of AD 49, making it possibly the earliest New Testament letter — which means James was wrestling with the application of the gospel to practical life before Paul had written most of his letters.

The letter draws deeply on the Sermon on the Mount, which James had presumably heard from Jesus himself, and on the Old Testament wisdom tradition — Proverbs, Job, the Psalms of lament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” — Jewish Christians scattered beyond Palestine, probably after the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1). These were people under pressure: economic hardship, social marginalization, the temptation to compromise, the fracturing of community under stress.

James’s relationship to Paul is complementary, not contradictory. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (Rom 4); James says Abraham was justified by works (Jas 2:21). The difference is not in the content of justification but in its reference point: Paul speaks of justification before God in the court of heaven (the forensic verdict of “righteous” that comes through faith alone); James speaks of justification before men in the arena of visible life (the demonstration that faith is genuine, which appears in its works). Both agree that dead faith saves no one; both agree that living faith produces fruit. Paul says faith alone justifies; James says the faith that justifies is never alone.

Read James as the letter that will not let you be comfortable with a merely intellectual Christianity. It asks the hardest questions: Does your faith survive under pressure? Does it make you generous? Does it control your tongue? Does it make you humble? Does it make you pray? These are not questions about earning salvation but about whether what you call faith is the real thing. James is not offering a second route to justification; he is describing what justification produces in the life of the one who has genuinely received it. It produces the kind of faith that works — which is the only kind that is faith at all.

1.title: Tested and Proven: Trials, Wisdom, and the Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 sets out the letter’s concern: real faith under pressure. James starts with circumstance, not doctrine. His readers are in trials, and in God’s hands trials produce what nothing else can: tested faith, steadfastness and maturity.

Three threads run through the chapter: trials and the faith they prove (vv. 2–12); temptation, which comes from our own desires, not from God, the unchanging giver of every good gift (vv. 13–18); and the word of God, which gives new birth, must be done and not only heard, and produces pure religion (vv. 19–27). The key word is “perfect” or “complete” (vv. 4, 17, 25): not flawless, but whole. Its opposite is the double-minded man (v. 8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Trials, Wisdom, and the God Who Does Not Change
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James, a servant of Christ, writes to scattered believers. Count trials joy, because tested faith produces steadfastness and maturity. If you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously, but ask without being double-minded. Poor and rich alike should boast in what God has made them. The one who endures will receive the crown of life. God never tempts anyone; temptation comes from our own desire and ends in death. But every good gift comes from the unchanging Father of lights, who gave us new birth by the word of truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing and Tempting

God tests to prove and strengthen; he never tempts. Temptation comes from our own desire, while every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who does not change.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were scattered believers under real pressure and real poverty.

Now: Counting trials joy is a judgment about what they produce, and it can be made while we are still in pain.

verseByVerse.quote: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.

Meaning first. James 1 introduces the letter’s great theme: genuine faith shows itself in a whole, consistent life. It begins with trials (vv. 2–4): meet them with joy, because the testing of faith produces endurance, and endurance leads to maturity. If anyone lacks the wisdom to handle trials, he should ask God, who gives generously, but ask in faith, not with a divided mind (vv. 5–8). Both poor and rich should see their situation in God’s light: the poor are exalted, the rich will fade like grass (vv. 9–11). Those who endure trial will receive the crown of life (v. 12). But no one should blame God for temptation; temptation arises from our own desires, which conceive sin and give birth to death, while God gives only good gifts and has brought us to new birth by his word (vv. 13–18). So be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to anger, get rid of filth, and humbly receive the implanted word that can save (vv. 19–21). And do not merely hear the word; do it. A hearer who does not act is like someone who looks in a mirror and forgets his face; the one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and acts will be blessed (vv. 22–25). True religion is not just talk but bridling the tongue, caring for orphans and widows, and keeping oneself unstained by the world (vv. 26–27).

Setting and background. James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection (Mark 6:3; John 7:5; 1 Corinthians 15:7) and became the leading elder of the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13–21; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). He was known as “James the Just” for his righteousness and prayerfulness; tradition says his knees were like a camel’s from kneeling in prayer. He was martyred around AD 62, according to the Jewish historian Josephus. The letter was probably written in the 40s, making it one of the earliest New Testament writings. It is very practical, with many echoes of Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount, and resembles Old Testament wisdom literature like Proverbs.

James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Servant” (doulos, slave, bondservant). Remarkably humble: the brother of Jesus does not mention his family relationship but calls himself Jesus’ slave. “The Lord Jesus Christ”: James, who once thought his brother was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), now calls him Lord and Messiah. The resurrection changed everything. God and Jesus are named together as the one master he serves.

To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. Key words. “Twelve tribes”: the whole people of God. “Dispersion” (diaspora, scattering): Jews living outside the land of Israel. Here probably Jewish Christians scattered abroad, perhaps after the persecution following Stephen’s death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). The church, made up of Jewish and later Gentile believers, is the renewed Israel, God’s people scattered as pilgrims in the world (1 Peter 1:1).

Greetings. Key words. “Greetings” (chairein, rejoice). The standard Greek letter opening, used also in the letter James helped draft in Acts 15:23. It leads directly to the next word, “joy” (v. 2), a wordplay: chairein… charan.

Where Christians differ: was James a full brother of Jesus? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, so that the “brothers” of Jesus were cousins or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage. Verdict: The most natural reading of the New Testament is that James was a younger half-brother of Jesus, a son of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph did not know Mary “until” she had given birth, and Jesus is called her “firstborn” (Luke 2:7). The Gospels name his brothers and mention sisters alongside Mary (Mark 6:3). The doctrine of perpetual virginity is not taught in Scripture. This does not lessen Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord.

What it does not mean. “Servant” does not mean James was a lesser follower. It expresses his complete devotion. Nor does addressing the twelve tribes mean the letter is only for ethnic Jews; it is Scripture for the whole church.

In a sentence. From James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to God’s people scattered among the nations: greetings.

For worship. If even Jesus’ own brother called him Lord, worship him today as your Lord and Master.
verseByVerse.note: James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church. He was put to death about AD 62. “The Dispersion” means Jewish believers scattered outside the land of Israel. The letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Count it all joy, my brothers. Key words. “Count” (hēgēsasthe, consider, regard, think of it as). A deliberate decision of the mind, not a feeling. “All joy” (pasan charan, pure joy, nothing but joy). Not joy in the trial itself, but in what God does through it. “My brothers”: affectionate, used fifteen times in the letter.

When you meet trials of various kinds. Key words. “Meet” (peripesēte, fall into, encounter unexpectedly, as the man who fell among thieves, Luke 10:30). Trials come suddenly, without choosing. “Trials” (peirasmois): the same Greek word can mean trials (external hardships) or temptations (inner enticements to sin). Here, trials. “Various kinds” (poikilois, many-coloured, diverse): poverty, persecution, illness, loss, conflict.

For you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. Key words. “Testing” (dokimion, proving, as metal is tested by fire to show it is genuine and to refine it, 1 Peter 1:7). “Produces” (katergazetai, works out, achieves). “Steadfastness” (hypomonēn, endurance, patience under pressure, the ability to remain under a load without collapsing). Trials are God’s gymnasium for faith (Romans 5:3–4).

And let steadfastness have its full effect. Key words. “Full effect” (ergon teleion, perfect work, complete result). Do not cut the process short by giving up or seeking escape at any cost.

That you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. Key words. “Perfect” (teleioi, mature, fully grown). “Complete” (holoklēroi, whole in every part, with nothing missing). “Lacking in nothing” (en mēdeni leipomenoi). The goal is maturity: a Christian character fully formed, like Christ. Not sinless perfection in this life, but wholeness and maturity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pretend trials do not hurt, or enjoy pain itself, or seek out suffering. Jesus wept and agonised (John 11:35; Luke 22:44). It means we can rejoice, even through tears, because God is using the trial for our good (Romans 8:28; Hebrews 12:11).

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, whenever you run into trials of many kinds, treat it as an occasion for pure joy, because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance finish its work, so that you may be mature and whole, not lacking anything.

On a Tuesday. What trial are you facing right now? Ask God: what endurance and maturity are you building in me through this? Then thank him, by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.

If any of you lacks wisdom. Key words. “Lacks” (leipetai), a wordplay with “lacking in nothing” (v. 4). If you lack anything, it is probably wisdom. “Wisdom” (sophias): not intellectual knowledge, but the practical skill of living rightly before God, seeing life from his point of view, especially in trials (Proverbs 1:7; 2:6; James 3:13–18). In trials, we need wisdom to understand and respond rightly.

Let him ask God. Key words. “Ask” (aiteitō, keep asking). Wisdom is God’s gift, given in answer to prayer (1 Kings 3:9–12; Proverbs 2:3–6).

Who gives generously to all without reproach. Key words. “Generously” (haplōs, simply, single-mindedly, without hesitation, freely). God gives with an open hand and a whole heart. “Without reproach” (mē oneidizontos, without scolding, without finding fault). He does not make us feel stupid for asking or remind us of past failures. He is not like a grudging human benefactor who gives with a lecture.

And it will be given him. Key words. A promise (Matthew 7:7–11).

But let him ask in faith, with no doubting. Key words. “In faith” (en pistei): trusting God’s character and promise. “Doubting” (diakrinomenos, being divided, wavering, debating with oneself). Not honest questions or struggles, but a divided heart that is not sure whether to trust God or to rely on something else.

For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. Key words. “Driven” (anemizomenō, blown by the wind). “Tossed” (rhipizomenō, tossed about, fanned). A vivid image from life near the sea: constantly moving, never stable, at the mercy of every wind (Ephesians 4:14; Isaiah 57:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean any flicker of doubt cancels prayer. The father who said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” was answered (Mark 9:24). The doubting here is a settled double-mindedness, not trusting God wholeheartedly. Nor does it mean God will give whatever we ask if we only believe hard enough; the promise is for wisdom, and God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14).

In a sentence. If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God for it. He gives freely to everyone and does not scold you for asking, and it will be given to you. But when you ask, you must believe and not waver, because a person who wavers is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.

On a Tuesday. What decision or trial do you need wisdom for? Ask God for it today, trusting that he will give it generously.

verseByVerse.quote: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord. Key words. “Suppose” (oiesthō, think, imagine). The person who prays with a divided heart should not expect an answer. Not because God is stingy, but because such a person is not truly trusting him.

He is a double-minded man. Key words. “Double-minded” (dipsychos, two-souled, with two minds). A word perhaps coined by James, used again in 4:8. One part of him wants God; another part wants the world or self-reliance. He tries to serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). Contrast God, who gives “simply,” single-mindedly (v. 5).

Unstable in all his ways. Key words. “Unstable” (akatastatos, restless, unsettled, disorderly), used of the tongue in 3:8. Double-mindedness in prayer spreads to the whole of life. Such a person is inconsistent everywhere.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God ignores weak or struggling believers. He hears the cry of the weak. It means a heart deliberately divided between God and something else cannot expect to receive from him.

In a sentence. That kind of person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. Such a person is divided in loyalty and unstable in everything they do.

On a Tuesday. Is your heart divided between trusting God and trusting something else? Ask him to make your heart whole and single toward him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation. Key words. “Lowly” (tapeinos, humble, poor, of low status). “Boast” (kauchasthō, rejoice, take pride). “Exaltation” (hypsei, high position). The poor believer may be despised by the world, but in Christ he is raised to the highest status: a child of God, an heir of the kingdom (2:5). Poverty is a trial (v. 2); faith sees it from God’s viewpoint.

And the rich in his humiliation. Key words. “Humiliation” (tapeinōsei, low position, being brought low). The rich believer must glory in his humbling: that in Christ, he stands on the same level as the poorest, a sinner saved by grace, and that his wealth gives him no standing before God. And perhaps also in the trials that humble him. The world’s values are reversed in God’s kingdom (Luke 1:52–53; 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

Because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. Key words. From Isaiah 40:6–8. “Pass away” (pareleusetai). Wealth and the rich person alike are temporary.

For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass. Key words. “Scorching heat” (kausōni, burning heat, or the hot east wind, the sirocco, which could wither vegetation in a single day in Palestine). Wild flowers bloom brilliantly in spring, then wither in days.

Its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. Key words. “Beauty” (euprepeia, the grace of its appearance). However beautiful, it does not last.

So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits. Key words. “Fade away” (maranthēsetai, wither, die out). “Pursuits” (poreiais, journeys, business trips, ways). He dies while still busy with his business deals (Luke 12:16–21). Wealth does not protect from death.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all rich people are unbelievers or that wealth is sinful. James addresses a rich “brother” (if “brother” applies to both). It means wealth is temporary and gives no standing before God, while the poor believer has an eternal inheritance.

In a sentence. The believer in humble circumstances should take pride in their high position in Christ, and the rich should take pride in being brought low, because the rich will pass away like a wild flower. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the plant; its blossom falls and its beauty is gone. In the same way, the rich will fade away even while they go about their business.

On a Tuesday. If you are poor, rejoice in your riches in Christ. If you are well off, hold your wealth loosely and remember it will fade.

parallels.desc: The grass withers, the flower fades

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.

Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial. Key words. “Blessed” (makarios, happy, fortunate, approved by God), as in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12). “Remains steadfast” (hypomenei, endures, perseveres), the verb form of “steadfastness” (v. 3). “Trial” (peirasmon).

For when he has stood the test. Key words. “Stood the test” (dokimos genomenos, having become approved, proved genuine). Like metal that passes the refiner’s test.

He will receive the crown of life. Key words. “Crown” (stephanon): the victor’s wreath (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4; Revelation 2:10). “Of life”: the crown that consists of eternal life. Not an extra reward on top of eternal life, but eternal life itself as the prize.

Which God has promised to those who love him. Key words. “Those who love him”: a description of true believers (2:5; Romans 8:28; 1 Corinthians 2:9). Love for God shows itself in endurance. Those who love him do not abandon him when trials come.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is earned by enduring. It is God’s promised gift to those who love him. Endurance is the evidence of genuine love and faith, which God himself produces (v. 3).

In a sentence. Happy is the person who keeps going under trial, because when they have passed the test they will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him.

For worship. Thank God for the crown of life he has promised you. Let that hope strengthen you to endure today.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.

Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God. Key words. Now peirazō shifts meaning from “test” to “tempt”: an inner enticement to sin. The same circumstance can be a trial God uses for good or a temptation we yield to. Human beings have always blamed God for their sin. Adam blamed “the woman whom you gave to be with me” (Genesis 3:12).

For God cannot be tempted with evil. Key words. “Cannot be tempted” (apeirastos, untemptable, inexperienced in evil). God is utterly holy. Evil has no foothold in him, nothing in him responds to it.

And he himself tempts no one. Key words. God tests his people (Genesis 22:1) to prove and strengthen them, but he never entices anyone to sin. His purpose is always good.

But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Key words. “His own desire” (tēs idias epithymias, his own lust, craving). The source of temptation is within us. “Lured” (exelkomenos, dragged away, drawn out), a hunting image: an animal drawn out of its safe place. “Enticed” (deleazomenos, baited, hooked), a fishing image: a fish attracted by bait that hides the hook. Desire looks attractive; the hook is hidden.

Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin. Key words. Now a birth image. “Conceived” (syllabousa): when desire is welcomed and embraced by the will, it becomes pregnant. “Gives birth” (tiktei) to sin: the act.

And sin when it is fully grown brings forth death. Key words. “Fully grown” (apotelestheisa, brought to completion, matured). “Brings forth” (apokyei, gives birth to). The terrible genealogy: desire, then sin, then death (Romans 6:23). Sin is never satisfied; it grows until it kills.

Where Christians differ: if God is sovereign over all things, is he the author of sin? Some object that the Reformed view of God’s sovereignty makes God responsible for evil. Verdict: God is sovereign over all things, including the sinful acts of human beings, which he permits and overrules for his good purposes (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Yet he is never the author of sin, never tempts anyone, and never approves of evil. Sin arises from the creature’s own desires. God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both taught in Scripture and must both be held, even when we cannot fully explain how they fit together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean temptation itself is sin. Jesus was tempted without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when desire is embraced. Nor does it deny that Satan tempts us (Matthew 4:1–11); but he can only work through our own desires, and we remain responsible.

In a sentence. When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he does not tempt anyone. Instead, each person is tempted when they are dragged away and lured by their own desire. Then, once desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, gives birth to death.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted this week, do not blame God or circumstances. Recognise the bait, remember the hook, and kill the desire before it conceives.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Key words. “Do not be deceived” (mē planasthe, do not be led astray). Do not be misled into thinking God is the source of evil.

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above. Key words. “Good gift” (dosis agathē, the act of giving that is good) and “perfect gift” (dōrēma teleion, the gift itself that is complete). The line has a poetic rhythm in Greek, perhaps a quotation. Far from tempting us, God is the source of everything good. “From above” (anōthen): from heaven, from God.

Coming down from the Father of lights. Key words. “Father of lights”: God, the creator of the sun, moon and stars (Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 136:7–9). He is the source of all light, physical and spiritual.

With whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Key words. “Variation” (parallagē, change, alteration). “Shadow due to change” (tropēs aposkiasma, a shadow cast by turning, as the shadows of a sundial move, or as the moon waxes and wanes, or as the heavenly bodies rise and set). The lights God made change constantly; God himself never changes (Malachi 3:6; Hebrews 13:8). His goodness never wavers, never dims. This is God’s immutability.

Of his own will he brought us forth. Key words. “Of his own will” (boulētheis, having willed, having purposed). God’s sovereign choice. “Brought us forth” (apekyēsen, gave birth to), the same verb used of sin giving birth to death (v. 15). The contrast is stunning: sin gives birth to death; God gives birth to life. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 1:13; 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:3, 23).

By the word of truth. Key words. “Word of truth”: the gospel (Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 1:5). God uses the gospel as the means of new birth (1 Peter 1:23).

That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. Key words. “Firstfruits” (aparchēn): the first part of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge that the whole harvest belongs to him (Leviticus 23:10). Believers are the first part of God’s new creation; the whole renewed creation will follow (Romans 8:19–23). Early Jewish Christians were literally among the first.

What it does not mean. “Of his own will he brought us forth” does not mean our response is unreal. We truly believe. But our new birth originates in God’s sovereign will, not in our decision (John 1:13). Regeneration precedes and produces faith. This is effectual calling.

In a sentence. Don’t be fooled, my dear brothers and sisters. Every good and perfect gift comes down from above, from the Father who made the lights in the sky, who does not change like their shifting shadows. He chose to give us new birth through the message of truth, so that we might be the first part of the harvest of everything he created.

For worship. Thank God for every good gift in your life today, and above all for the new birth he gave you by his own will.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger, because human anger does not produce God’s righteousness. Put off moral filth and humbly receive the word planted in you, which can save you. Do not only hear the word but do it. The hearer who does nothing is like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face; the doer who keeps looking into the law of liberty is blessed. Religion that cannot control the tongue is worthless. Pure religion is caring for orphans and widows and keeping oneself unstained by the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mirror

Hearing without doing is self-deception. The blessed man looks into the perfect law of liberty, stays there, and acts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Orphans and widows were the people with no one to speak for them.

Now: Pure religion still means turning up for the helpless and keeping unstained from the world — both, not one.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.

Know this, my beloved brothers. Key words. “Know this” (iste): either “you know this” or “take note of this.” A new section begins: responding rightly to the word of truth (v. 18).

Let every person be quick to hear. Key words. “Quick” (tachys, swift, ready, eager). “Hear” (akousai, listen). Especially to God’s word, but also to others. Eager to listen and learn.

Slow to speak. Key words. “Slow” (bradys). Not silent, but careful, thoughtful, not rushing to give opinions, especially in disputes (Proverbs 10:19; 17:27–28). James will develop the dangers of the tongue in chapter 3.

Slow to anger. Key words. “Anger” (orgēn, wrath, settled indignation). Hasty speech often leads to anger, and anger to more hasty speech. God himself is slow to anger (Exodus 34:6). In trials, it is easy to become angry with God, with others, with circumstances.

For the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Key words. “Produce” (ergazetai, work out, accomplish). “Righteousness of God”: the righteous life God requires and desires. Human anger does not achieve God’s righteous purposes. We may think our anger is justified and will fix things, but it usually makes things worse.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all anger. There is righteous anger at sin and injustice (Ephesians 4:26; Mark 3:5). But human anger is usually mixed with pride and self-interest, and it must not be quick.

In a sentence. My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteous life that God desires.

On a Tuesday. In your next conversation, especially a difficult one, practise: listen fully first, speak slowly, and let anger wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

Therefore put away all filthiness. Key words. “Put away” (apothemenoi, take off, strip off, as dirty clothes), as in Ephesians 4:22, 25; Colossians 3:8; 1 Peter 2:1; Hebrews 12:1. “Filthiness” (rhyparian, moral dirt, defilement; the word was also used of earwax, which blocks hearing). Sin blocks our ears to God’s word.

And rampant wickedness. Key words. “Rampant” (perisseian, abundance, overflow, excess). “Wickedness” (kakias, malice, evil). The excess of evil that remains even in believers.

And receive with meekness the implanted word. Key words. “Receive” (dexasthe, welcome, accept). “Meekness” (prautēti, humility, gentleness, teachableness): the opposite of anger. A humble, teachable spirit that submits to God’s word. “Implanted” (emphyton, planted in, rooted, ingrafted). The word of truth (v. 18) has been planted in believers at their new birth (Jeremiah 31:33). Now they must keep receiving it, letting it grow.

Which is able to save your souls. Key words. “Able” (dynamenon, has power). “Save your souls”: the final salvation of the whole person (5:20; 1 Peter 1:9). The word that gave new birth continues to work, bringing believers through to final salvation. God saves through his word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved at all. They have been born again (v. 18). But salvation has past, present and future aspects: we have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved. The word keeps working until the end.

In a sentence. So get rid of all moral filth and the evil that is so widespread, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save you.

On a Tuesday. What sin is blocking your ears to God’s word? Strip it off, and come to Scripture this week with a humble, teachable heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

But be doers of the word. Key words. “Be” (ginesthe, become, keep on being). “Doers” (poiētai, makers, performers, practitioners; our word “poet”). Receiving the word (v. 21) must lead to doing it. This is perhaps the key verse of the letter.

And not hearers only. Key words. “Hearers” (akroatai, listeners, audience members, those who attend lectures). In the synagogue and church, Scripture was read aloud; it was possible to listen regularly and never act. Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with the same warning (Matthew 7:24–27).

Deceiving yourselves. Key words. “Deceiving” (paralogizomenoi, reasoning falsely, miscalculating, deluding). The hearer who does not act thinks hearing is enough. He deceives himself into thinking he is spiritual because he knows the truth. But knowledge without obedience is self-deception.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is by doing. James will show that genuine faith always works (2:14–26). The doing is the evidence of genuine hearing, the fruit of the implanted word.

In a sentence. Do not merely listen to the word and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.

On a Tuesday. Take one thing you heard from Scripture last Sunday. What specific action does it call for? Do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.

For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer. Key words. An illustration.

He is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. Key words. “Looks intently” (katanoounti, observes, considers). “Natural face” (to prosōpon tēs geneseōs autou, the face of his birth, the face he was born with). “Mirror” (esoptrō): ancient mirrors were polished metal, usually bronze, giving an imperfect reflection. Scripture is like a mirror: it shows us what we really are.

For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like. Key words. “Goes away” (apelēlythen, perfect tense: has gone off). “At once forgets” (eutheōs epelatheto). He sees a smudge on his face, then walks away and does nothing about it. A brief glance, no action. So the hearer sees his sin in Scripture, feels briefly convicted, and walks away unchanged.

What it does not mean. It does not mean looking at ourselves in Scripture is bad. It is essential. The problem is looking and doing nothing.

In a sentence. Anyone who listens to the word but does not do what it says is like someone who looks at their face in a mirror and, after looking, goes away and immediately forgets what they look like.

On a Tuesday. When Scripture shows you something about yourself this week, don’t walk away. Stop and respond: confess, change, act.

verseByVerse.quote: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.

But the one who looks into the perfect law. Key words. “Looks into” (parakypsas, stoops down to look, peers into intently), the word used of Peter and John stooping to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5, 11) and of angels longing to look into salvation (1 Peter 1:12). Not a quick glance but a deep, careful gaze. “Perfect law” (nomon teleion, complete, mature law): God’s word, including the moral law as fulfilled and interpreted by Christ, the royal law of love (2:8).

The law of liberty. Key words. “Liberty” (eleutherias, freedom). A surprising phrase: law that gives freedom. Not because it removes all obligations, but because it is written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33), and obeyed from love, not compulsion. True freedom is the freedom to do what is right, freed from slavery to sin (John 8:31–36; Romans 8:2). The law of liberty also judges (2:12).

And perseveres. Key words. “Perseveres” (parameinas, remains, continues). He keeps looking, keeps applying, does not walk away.

Being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts. Key words. Literally “not a hearer of forgetfulness but a doer of work.” A Hebrew way of speaking: a forgetful hearer versus an effective doer.

He will be blessed in his doing. Key words. “Blessed” (makarios), as in verse 12. The blessing comes in the doing (John 13:17; Psalm 1:1–3). Not after it, as a reward earned, but in the very act of obedience, God’s blessing is experienced.

What it does not mean. “Law of liberty” does not mean Christians are free to ignore God’s commands. It means God’s commands, written on the heart, set us free to live as we were made to live. Nor does blessing for doing mean salvation by works; it is the blessing of a life in step with God.

In a sentence. But whoever looks closely into the perfect law that gives freedom, and keeps on doing so, not forgetting what they have heard but putting it into practice, will be blessed in what they do.

For worship. Look deeply into God’s word today, and thank him that his law, written on your heart, gives you real freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.

If anyone thinks he is religious. Key words. “Thinks” (dokei, supposes, seems to himself). “Religious” (thrēskos, devout, observing religious practices, worship and ritual). He attends worship, prays, fasts, and considers himself spiritual.

And does not bridle his tongue. Key words. “Bridle” (chalinagōgōn, guide with a bridle, rein in), an image developed in 3:2–3. An uncontrolled tongue (gossip, slander, harshness, lies) contradicts religious claims.

But deceives his heart. Key words. “Deceives” (apatōn). Self-deception again (v. 22).

This person’s religion is worthless. Key words. “Worthless” (mataios, empty, futile, vain). All the outward religious activity is empty if the tongue is unrestrained.

Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this. Key words. “Pure” (kathara, clean) and “undefiled” (amiantos, unstained), terms of ritual purity. But James redefines purity: not ritual cleanness, but practical love and moral holiness. “Before God the Father”: what God, not people, counts as genuine.

To visit orphans and widows in their affliction. Key words. “Visit” (episkeptesthai, look after, care for, see to the needs of; the root of “overseer”). Orphans and widows were the most vulnerable in society, with no one to provide for them or defend them. God is their defender (Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 68:5). True religion cares for those who cannot repay.

And to keep oneself unstained from the world. Key words. “Unstained” (aspilon, spotless). “The world” (tou kosmou): human society organised in rebellion against God, with its values, desires and pressures (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17). True religion is both outward love and inward holiness: compassion for the needy and separation from worldliness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean caring for the needy is the whole of religion, or that worship and doctrine do not matter. James assumes faith in Christ (2:1). He is showing what genuine faith looks like in practice, as opposed to empty ritual.

In a sentence. Those who consider themselves religious but do not keep a tight rein on their tongues are fooling themselves, and their religion is worthless. The religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

On a Tuesday. Is there an orphan, widow, or vulnerable person you could help this week? And is there a worldly influence you need to cut off?
