2.title: No Partiality: Faith That Sees Every Person
2.overview:
Chapter 2 has two movements, closely linked. The first (vv. 1–13) confronts favouritism in the church: welcoming the rich visitor to a good seat and sending the poor man to the floor. The second (vv. 14–26) asks what real faith is: a faith that produces no works is dead. The link is the poor visitor. A faith that produces no love for him is exactly the dead faith of vv. 14–26.

James is not opposing Paul’s gospel. He is opposing a counterfeit of it: the idea that agreeing with correct doctrine is the same as saving faith. Even demons believe that God is one. What saves is living faith in Christ, shown in Abraham offering Isaac and Rahab sheltering the spies. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Gold Ring and the Royal Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not hold faith in the glorious Lord Jesus while showing favouritism. James stages a scene: a man with a gold ring is given a good seat, a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor. That makes you corrupt judges. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich oppress you. Favouritism breaks the royal law of love, and breaking one command makes you guilty before the one Lawgiver. So speak and act as those who will be judged, for mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Lawgiver

Partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory and breaks the royal law. Whoever fails at one point stands guilty before the one who spoke the whole law — and mercy triumphs over judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregation seated the man with the gold ring well and the poor man on the floor.

Now: The sin is not only exclusion but ranking people inside a real welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.

Meaning first. James 2 has two linked parts, both showing that genuine faith works itself out in love. First, a warning against favouritism (vv. 1–13). Faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot coexist with snobbery. If the church fawns over a rich visitor and humiliates a poor one, it has become a court of corrupt judges (vv. 1–4). God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, while the rich are often those who oppress believers and slander Christ’s name (vv. 5–7). The royal law is to love your neighbour as yourself; favouritism breaks it, and breaking one command makes you guilty of the whole law (vv. 8–11). So speak and act as those who will be judged by the law of liberty, remembering that judgement is merciless to those who show no mercy, and mercy triumphs over judgement (vv. 12–13). Second, the famous passage on faith and works (vv. 14–26). A faith that says the right words but does nothing for a hungry brother is useless and dead (vv. 14–17). Faith is shown by works; even demons believe that God is one, and shudder (vv. 18–19). Abraham’s faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac, fulfilling the Scripture that he believed God and was counted righteous; so a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (vv. 20–24). Rahab too showed her faith by her actions; faith without works is as dead as a body without breath (vv. 25–26). James is not contradicting Paul: both teach that saving faith is a living faith that produces works, and that a mere profession without works is not saving faith at all.

My brothers, show no partiality. Key words. “Partiality” (prosōpolēmpsiais, receiving the face, judging by appearance, favouritism). A Hebrew idiom: lifting up someone’s face, showing favour on the basis of outward appearance, wealth or status. God shows no partiality (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11), and his people must not either (Leviticus 19:15).

As you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Hold” (echete, have, possess). “The faith in our Lord Jesus Christ”: faith that trusts in Christ. James clearly assumes faith in Christ as the foundation of the Christian life. Favouritism contradicts that faith.

The Lord of glory. Key words. Literally “our Lord Jesus Christ of the glory.” Jesus is the glorious one, the Shekinah, God’s glory dwelling among us (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 2:8; Hebrews 1:3). In the presence of his glory, human distinctions of wealth and rank are meaningless. How could anyone who believes in the Lord of glory fawn over a man’s gold ring? This also implies his deity: glory belongs to God alone (Isaiah 42:8).

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all distinctions, such as honouring elders or respecting authorities (Romans 13:7). It forbids treating people differently because of wealth, status, race or appearance, especially in the church.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favouritism.

On a Tuesday. Notice whom you are naturally drawn to at church and whom you overlook. This Sunday, go out of your way to welcome someone you might normally ignore.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing. Key words. “Gold ring” (chrysodaktylios, gold-fingered): perhaps wearing many rings, a sign of wealth, or the ring of the Roman equestrian class. “Fine clothing” (esthēti lampra, bright, shining, splendid clothes).

Comes into your assembly. Key words. “Assembly” (synagōgēn, synagogue, gathering). The only place in the New Testament where a Christian meeting is called a synagogue, reflecting the Jewish background of James’s readers. It may refer to a worship service or a church court gathered to settle disputes (1 Corinthians 6:1–6).

And a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in. Key words. “Shabby” (rhypara, filthy, dirty), the same root as “filthiness” in 1:21. Perhaps the only clothes he owned.

And if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing. Key words. “Pay attention” (epiblepsēte, look upon with favour, gaze admiringly).

And say, You sit here in a good place. Key words. “Good place” (kalōs, comfortably, in a place of honour).

While you say to the poor man, You stand over there, or, Sit down at my feet. Key words. “At my feet” (hypo to hypopodion mou, under my footstool): on the floor, like a servant or a dog. A deliberate humiliation.

Have you not then made distinctions among yourselves. Key words. “Made distinctions” (diekrithēte, discriminated, been divided). The same word as “doubting” (1:6). Favouritism reveals a divided heart, double-mindedness.

And become judges with evil thoughts? Key words. “Judges with evil thoughts” (kritai dialogismōn ponērōn, judges whose reasoning is wicked). They have set themselves up as judges of people’s worth, and their standards are corrupt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should never show courtesy to visitors, rich or poor. It means it must not show greater honour on the basis of wealth or appearance.

In a sentence. Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in filthy old clothes also comes in. If you show special attention to the man in fine clothes and say, “Here’s a good seat for you,” but say to the poor man, “You stand there,” or “Sit on the floor by my feet,” have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with wicked motives?

On a Tuesday. How does your church welcome the poor, the shabby, the awkward? Ask how you could personally help make them feel honoured.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?

Listen, my beloved brothers. Key words. “Listen” (akousate): pay attention.

Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world. Key words. “Chosen” (exelexato, elected, selected). God’s sovereign choice in salvation (1 Corinthians 1:26–29; Ephesians 1:4). “Poor in the world” (tous ptōchous tō kosmō, poor in the world’s eyes, by worldly standards). God has often chosen the poor, as the early church was mostly made up of the poor (Luke 6:20; 1 Corinthians 1:26).

To be rich in faith. Key words. Poor in the world, rich in faith. True riches are spiritual.

And heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? Key words. “Heirs” (klēronomous). “Kingdom”: God’s reign, now and fully in the age to come (Matthew 5:3; 25:34). “Those who love him”: as in 1:12. The poor believer is a future king.

But you have dishonored the poor man. Key words. “Dishonored” (ētimasate, shamed, insulted). Those whom God has honoured, the church has shamed.

Are not the rich the ones who oppress you. Key words. “Oppress” (katadynasteuousin, exercise power over, exploit, tyrannise). Wealthy landowners and creditors often exploited the poor (5:1–6).

And the ones who drag you into court? Key words. “Drag” (helkousin, haul, pull by force). Perhaps over debts, or because of their faith (Acts 16:19).

Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called? Key words. “Blaspheme” (blasphēmousin, slander, revile). “Honorable name” (to kalon onoma, the good, beautiful name): the name of Christ. “By which you were called” (to epiklēthen eph’ hymas, which was called over you): perhaps at baptism, when Christ’s name was pronounced over the believer, marking them as his (Acts 2:38). Why fawn over people who mock your Lord?

What it does not mean. It does not mean every rich person is wicked or every poor person is saved. God saves rich and poor alike by grace. James is speaking generally of the rich unbelievers who oppressed the church. Nor does it mean poverty itself is a virtue; it is a hardship in which God’s grace often shines.

In a sentence. Listen, my dear brothers and sisters: has God not chosen those who are poor in the world’s eyes to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised those who love him? But you have insulted the poor. Is it not the rich who exploit you? Are they not the ones dragging you into court? Are they not the ones slandering the noble name of him to whom you belong?

For worship. Thank God that he chooses the poor and despised. Ask him to give you his eyes for the poor in your church and community.

verseByVerse.quote: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.

If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture. Key words. “Really” (mentoi, indeed). “Fulfill” (teleite, carry out, accomplish). “Royal law” (nomon basilikon, kingly law, the law of the kingdom). Royal because it is the supreme law, given by the King, Jesus himself, who called it the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and because it belongs to the kingdom (v. 5).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Key words. From Leviticus 19:18. Notably, Leviticus 19:15 just before it forbids partiality in judgement. Love of neighbour sums up the second table of the law (Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14).

You are doing well. Key words. “Doing well” (kalōs poieite). Perhaps the favouritists claimed they were loving the rich man as a neighbour. James says: if you truly love your neighbour, all your neighbours, you do well.

But if you show partiality, you are committing sin. Key words. “Show partiality” (prosōpolēmpteite). Favouritism is not a minor social failure; it is sin (hamartian).

And are convicted by the law as transgressors. Key words. “Convicted” (elenchomenoi, exposed, proved guilty). “Transgressors” (parabatai, those who step over the line). The same law they claim to keep convicts them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love of neighbour replaces love of God. The first great commandment remains first. But love of God shows itself in love of neighbour (1 John 4:20).

In a sentence. If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, “Love your neighbour as yourself,” you are doing right. But if you show favouritism, you sin, and the law convicts you as lawbreakers.

On a Tuesday. Who is the neighbour you find hardest to love as yourself? Do one practical act of love for them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.

For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point. Key words. “Fails” (ptaisē, stumbles, trips). Even a single failure.

Has become guilty of all of it. Key words. “Guilty” (enochos, liable, answerable). The law is a unity, like a single sheet of glass: crack it anywhere and the whole is broken. It is not a collection of separate rules, where breaking one leaves the others untouched. It is the expression of one will, one God.

For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. Key words. From the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:13–14; Deuteronomy 5:17–18). The same God gave both. To break either is to defy him.

If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. Key words. You cannot excuse breaking one command by boasting about keeping another. The favouritists might pride themselves on avoiding adultery and murder, but by favouritism they have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all sins are equally serious in every respect. Scripture recognises degrees of sin and punishment (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48). It means that any sin makes us lawbreakers before God, guilty and in need of grace. No one can be justified by law-keeping (Galatians 3:10; Romans 3:19–20). This drives us to Christ, who kept the whole law perfectly for us.

In a sentence. For anyone who keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. The one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do commit murder, you have still broken the law.

For worship. Thank Christ that he kept the whole law perfectly in your place, and that his righteousness is counted as yours.

verseByVerse.quote: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

So speak and so act. Key words. “Speak” (laleite) and “act” (poieite): both words and deeds, present tense: keep doing so. James joins speech and action throughout the letter.

As those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. Key words. “Are to be judged” (mellontes krinesthai, are about to be judged). Believers will stand before God’s judgement, not to determine salvation, but to evaluate their lives (Romans 14:10–12; 2 Corinthians 5:10). “Law of liberty” (1:25): the law of love, written on the heart. This law sets free, but it also judges: those who have been set free are expected to live accordingly.

For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Key words. “Without mercy” (aneleos, merciless). Jesus taught the same (Matthew 5:7; 6:14–15; 18:21–35, the unforgiving servant). Those who show no mercy reveal that they have never truly received God’s mercy.

Mercy triumphs over judgment. Key words. “Triumphs” (katakauchatai, boasts over, exults over, gains the victory). God’s mercy, received and shown, wins over judgement. For those who have received mercy in Christ and show it to others, the judgement holds no terror. Mercy shown to others is the evidence that we have received mercy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s mercy by showing mercy. We show mercy because we have received it (Ephesians 4:32). But a merciless life is evidence of an unrenewed heart.

In a sentence. Speak and act as people who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom, because judgement without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgement.

On a Tuesday. To whom do you need to show mercy this week? Forgive, help, or give, remembering the mercy God has shown you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What good is it to say you have faith if you have no works? Can that kind of faith save? Words of blessing to a hungry brother with no food given are useless; faith without works is dead. Even demons believe that God is one, and tremble. Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, and his faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac. Rahab’s faith was shown when she hid the spies. As the body without breath is dead, so faith without works is dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith That Works

James asks whether a faith that is only said can save. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and his obedience showed that faith to be alive. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the demons believe that God is one — and shudder.

Now: Warm words to a hungry brother with nothing given are the picture of dead faith.

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?

What good is it, my brothers. Key words. “What good” (ti to ophelos, what profit, what use). The theme of the passage: useful faith versus useless faith.

If someone says he has faith but does not have works? Key words. “Says” (legē): the key word. James is not describing real faith, but a claim to faith. A profession with no evidence. “Works” (erga): deeds of love and obedience, like caring for the poor (vv. 15–16), not the “works of the law” (circumcision, food laws, ritual) that Paul denies can justify.

Can that faith save him? Key words. “That faith” (hē pistis, the faith, with the article: this kind of faith, the faith just described). Greek grammar expects the answer “No.” A faith that consists only of words, with no works, cannot save.

Where Christians differ: does James contradict Paul? Paul says we are justified by faith, not works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16); James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (v. 24). Some have thought they contradict each other; Luther once called James “an epistle of straw” for this reason, though he later came to value it more. Roman Catholic teaching uses James to argue that justification includes good works. Verdict: They do not contradict. They are answering different errors and using key words in different senses. Paul opposes legalism: those who think they can earn God’s acceptance by works of the law. James opposes empty profession: those who think a faith with no fruit can save. For Paul, “justify” means God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous, received through faith alone. For James, “justify” here means to show or prove righteous, as Abraham’s faith was vindicated by his deeds. For Paul, “works” means works of the law done to earn merit; for James, works of love that flow from faith. For Paul, “faith” means genuine trust in Christ; for James, in verse 14, “faith” means a mere claim to believe. Both agree: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it always produces works (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean works are part of the ground of justification. Christ’s righteousness alone is the ground. It means works are the necessary evidence of genuine faith.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, what use is it if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds to show for it? Can that kind of faith save them?

On a Tuesday. If someone looked at your life this week, what evidence of faith would they see? Ask God to make your faith visible in love.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says we are justified by faith, not works; James says a faith that produces no works is not saving faith. They answer different errors.

verseByVerse.quote: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food. Key words. “Poorly clothed” (gymnoi, naked, inadequately dressed). “Lacking in daily food” (leipomenoi tēs ephēmerou trophēs, without food for the day). A fellow believer in desperate need. “Brother or sister”: James explicitly includes women.

And one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and filled. Key words. “Go in peace” (hypagete en eirēnē), a common Jewish farewell blessing. “Be warmed and filled” (thermainesthe kai chortazesthe): perhaps a pious wish, or even a prayer. Fine words, no action. The words are kind; the absence of help is cruel.

Without giving them the things needed for the body. Key words. Words cannot warm or feed.

What good is that? Key words. The same question as verse 14. Words without deeds are useless to the needy.

So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. Key words. “By itself” (kath’ heautēn, alone, on its own). “Dead” (nekra): not merely weak or immature, but lifeless. A faith that produces no works is not real, living faith. It is a corpse. Just as kind words without help are empty, so a profession of faith without works is empty (1 John 3:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith becomes alive by adding works, as if works give life to faith. Rather, works show that faith is alive. A living tree bears fruit; the fruit does not make it alive.

In a sentence. Suppose a brother or sister has no clothes and no food for the day. If one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat well,” but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith on its own, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have wished well but not helped? Move from words to action this week: give food, clothing, money or time.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!

But someone will say, You have faith and I have works. Key words. An imagined objector, perhaps arguing that faith and works are separate gifts: some people have faith, others have works, and both are fine. The exact boundaries of the quotation are debated, but the point is clear: James rejects separating faith and works.

Show me your faith apart from your works. Key words. “Show” (deixon, demonstrate, prove). A challenge: faith is invisible; how can you prove it exists without works? You cannot.

And I will show you my faith by my works. Key words. Works are the visible evidence of invisible faith. The only way to show faith is by its fruit (Matthew 7:16–20).

You believe that God is one; you do well. Key words. The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4): “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” Every devout Jew recited it daily. Believing it is good; it is true.

Even the demons believe—and shudder! Key words. “Believe” (pisteuousin): the demons hold correct doctrine. They know who God is, and who Jesus is (Mark 1:24; 5:7). “Shudder” (phrissousin, tremble, bristle with fear, the hair standing on end). They believe and tremble, but they do not trust, love or obey. Intellectual belief alone, even correct belief, is not saving faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean correct doctrine is unimportant. The demons are right about God. It means correct doctrine without trust, love and obedience is demonic, not saving. Saving faith includes knowledge, agreement and personal trust (the Reformers’ notitia, assensus, fiducia).

In a sentence. But someone will say, “You have faith; I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that there is one God. Good! Even the demons believe that, and they tremble with fear.

On a Tuesday. Beyond believing the right things about God, are you trusting him, loving him, obeying him? Let your faith go further than the demons’ faith.
verseByVerse.note: The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?

Do you want to be shown. Key words. “Want” (theleis, are you willing). “Shown” (gnōnai, know, recognise). James is about to give proof from Scripture.

You foolish person. Key words. “Foolish” (kene, empty, hollow, vain). A person whose faith is empty, without substance, matching his empty faith. Not an insult but a rebuke, like Jesus’ “O foolish ones” (Luke 24:25).

That faith apart from works is useless? Key words. “Useless” (argē, idle, unproductive, not working). A wordplay in Greek: faith without works (ergōn) does not work (a-ergē). Some manuscripts read “dead” (as in vv. 17, 26), but “useless” is better supported.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the person addressed is beyond hope. James rebukes in order to restore.

In a sentence. You foolish person, do you want proof that faith without deeds does not work?

For worship. Ask God to keep your faith from becoming empty, and to fill it with the substance of love and obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;

Was not Abraham our father justified by works. Key words. “Abraham our father”: the father of the Jewish people and of all who believe (Romans 4:11–12). “Justified” (edikaiōthē). Here the word means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine. Paul uses Abraham to prove justification by faith (Romans 4:1–5; Galatians 3:6); James uses him to prove that justifying faith works.

When he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? Key words. Genesis 22. Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22. So the offering of Isaac did not make Abraham righteous before God; he already was. It demonstrated and vindicated his faith. God said afterward: “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12). The test proved the faith genuine.

You see that faith was active along with his works. Key words. “Was active along with” (synērgei, worked together with, cooperated). Faith and works worked together. Faith was the source; works were the expression. Abraham’s faith did not sit idle; it went to work.

And faith was completed by his works. Key words. “Completed” (eteleiōthē, perfected, brought to its goal, matured). Not that faith was incomplete or deficient before, but that works brought it to its intended expression, as a seed is completed by producing fruit. Faith reached its full goal in obedience.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham was declared righteous before God because of his works. Scripture says he was counted righteous when he believed (Genesis 15:6), decades before Genesis 22. His works proved his faith genuine before God and others.

In a sentence. Was not our ancestor Abraham shown to be righteous by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith reached its full goal through what he did.

For worship. Thank God for giving you faith. Ask him to let it work together with your actions, so that it reaches its full goal.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Key words. From Genesis 15:6, the key verse Paul uses for justification by faith (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). “Was fulfilled” (eplērōthē, filled up, brought to full meaning). Genesis 15:6 was the initial declaration; Genesis 22 filled it out, showing the genuineness of the faith that was counted as righteousness. “Counted” (elogisthē, reckoned, credited, imputed): a legal and accounting word. God credited righteousness to Abraham when he believed.

And he was called a friend of God. Key words. “Friend of God” (philos theou): a title given to Abraham (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8). Genuine faith leads to intimate relationship with God, shown in obedience (John 15:14–15).

You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Key words. The most debated phrase in James. “Justified” here, as in verse 21, means shown or vindicated as righteous. “Not by faith alone” (ouk ek pisteōs monon): not by the kind of faith described in verses 14–19, a faith that is alone, without works, a mere profession. Such “faith” does not justify, because it is not genuine faith. A person is shown to be righteous by works that prove the reality of their faith.

Where Christians differ: does this verse deny justification by faith alone? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse as proof against the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone. Verdict: James is not denying that we are declared righteous by faith alone in Paul’s sense; he quotes Genesis 15:6 himself. He is denying that a faith which remains alone, without works, is saving faith. The Reformers said it well: we are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. James and Paul agree: God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith in Christ, on the basis of his righteousness imputed to them; and the faith that receives this always works by love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our works merit God’s acceptance, or that justification is a lifelong process of becoming righteous. It means that genuine justifying faith is always shown by works.

In a sentence. And so the Scripture came true that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is shown to be righteous by what they do, and not by a faith that stays on its own.

For worship. Thank God that righteousness has been credited to you by faith, and that you are his friend. Show that friendship in obedience.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22; the offering showed the faith was real.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.

And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works. Key words. A deliberate contrast with Abraham. Abraham was a man, the patriarch, a Jew, the friend of God; Rahab was a woman, a Gentile, a Canaanite, a prostitute. Yet both had the same kind of faith, and both showed it by works. Genuine faith looks the same across every human distinction. Rahab is also commended in Hebrews 11:31.

When she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? Key words. “Received” (hypodexamenē, welcomed as guests). “Sent them out” (ekbalousa, thrust out, helped them escape) by a different route (Joshua 2:1–21). Her faith in Israel’s God (Joshua 2:9–11) led her to risk her life to protect his people. Her actions showed her faith was real.

For as the body apart from the spirit is dead. Key words. “Spirit” (pneumatos, breath, spirit). A body without breath, without spirit, is a corpse.

So also faith apart from works is dead. Key words. The conclusion of the passage, repeating verse 17. Faith without works is like a corpse: it has the form but not the life. Note the comparison: faith corresponds to the body, and works to the spirit. Works are the evidence of life in faith; without them, faith is dead.

What it does not mean. It does not commend Rahab’s former life or her lie (see Hebrews 11:31). It commends her faith-driven act of protecting God’s messengers. Nor does it make works the source of faith’s life; it makes them the sign of it.

In a sentence. In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute shown to be righteous by what she did when she welcomed the spies and sent them off in a different direction? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your background, your faith can be real and active. What risk might faith call you to take this week for God’s people?

3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Chapter 3 deals with two linked themes: the tongue and wisdom. The tongue (vv. 1–12) is small but decisive, like a bit, a rudder or a spark, and no human can tame it. Its problem is not speech but the heart: a spring gives what its source supplies.

So James turns to wisdom (vv. 13–18). Earthly wisdom, full of jealousy and selfish ambition, produces disorder. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, merciful, impartial and sincere, and it yields a harvest of righteousness sown in peace. The answer to the tongue is not a technique, but a new source.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not many should become teachers, because teachers are judged more strictly. We all stumble, and the one who controls his speech is mature. The tongue is small, like a bit or a rudder, but it steers everything; like a spark, it sets a forest ablaze. No human can tame it. With it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness, which ought not to be. A spring cannot give fresh and salt water from one opening.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Tongue Cannot Be Tamed

The tongue is small and decisive, and no human can tame it. The problem is the spring, not the water; the answer is wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in the congregation wanted to teach.

Now: We cannot bless God and curse people made in his likeness from the same mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.

Meaning first. James 3 develops two themes from chapter 1: the tongue (1:19, 26) and wisdom (1:5). First, the tongue (vv. 1–12). Teachers will be judged more strictly, because they use words, and everyone stumbles in speech; whoever never stumbles in speech is mature enough to control his whole self (vv. 1–2). The tongue is small but powerful, like a horse’s bit or a ship’s rudder (vv. 3–4). It is like a tiny spark that sets a forest ablaze; it is a world of evil among our members, defiling the whole person and setting life on fire, itself set on fire by hell (vv. 5–6). Every kind of animal has been tamed, but no human can tame the tongue: it is restless and full of deadly poison (vv. 7–8). With it we bless God and curse people made in his image, which should not happen; a spring does not pour out fresh and salt water, nor a fig tree bear olives (vv. 9–12). Second, two kinds of wisdom (vv. 13–18). True wisdom shows itself in good conduct and gentle humility (v. 13). Jealousy and selfish ambition are a false wisdom, earthly, unspiritual and demonic, producing disorder and every evil (vv. 14–16). The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, reasonable, merciful, fruitful, impartial and sincere, and peacemakers sow a harvest of righteousness (vv. 17–18).

Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers. Key words. “Teachers” (didaskaloi): those who teach in the church, a recognised and respected role (Acts 13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11). In Jewish culture, rabbis were highly honoured, and many wanted the status. James warns against seeking it lightly.

For you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness. Key words. “We”: James includes himself. “Greater strictness” (meizon krima, greater judgement, heavier condemnation). Teachers influence many; their words shape others’ beliefs and lives. They are responsible for both what they teach and how they live (Matthew 5:19; 12:36–37; Luke 12:48; Hebrews 13:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one should teach. The church needs teachers (2 Timothy 2:2). It means teaching is a serious responsibility not to be sought for status, and those who teach must be qualified and humble.

In a sentence. Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.

On a Tuesday. If you teach in any way, whether Sunday school, Bible study, parenting, or online, pray for faithfulness and humility, knowing you will give account.

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.

For we all stumble in many ways. Key words. “Stumble” (ptaiomen, trip, fall, make mistakes, sin), as in 2:10. “We all”: no exceptions, James included. “In many ways” (polla): many times, in many areas. Every believer continues to sin (1 John 1:8).

And if anyone does not stumble in what he says. Key words. “In what he says” (en logō, in word, in speech). The tongue is the hardest area to control.

He is a perfect man. Key words. “Perfect” (teleios, mature, complete), as in 1:4. Someone who never sins in speech would be fully mature. This is hypothetical: since we all stumble, no one has reached it.

Able also to bridle his whole body. Key words. “Bridle” (chalinagōgēsai, rein in, control), as in 1:26. If you can control your tongue, you can control everything else. The tongue is the test of self-control.

Where Christians differ: can a Christian reach sinless perfection in this life? Some holiness and Wesleyan traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state of freedom from conscious sin. Verdict: James says “we all stumble in many ways,” including himself, an apostolic leader. Scripture teaches that believers grow in holiness throughout life but are never sinless until glory (1 John 1:8–10; Philippians 3:12–14; Romans 7:14–25). We pursue maturity earnestly, but we always need daily forgiveness.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin because “we all stumble.” It humbles us and calls us to work at the hardest area, speech.

In a sentence. We all make many mistakes. Anyone who never makes a mistake in what they say is fully mature, able to keep their whole body in check.

For worship. Confess to God the ways you have stumbled in speech this week, and thank him for forgiveness in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.

If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us. Key words. “Bits” (chalinous, bridles, bits). A small piece of metal in a horse’s mouth controls a powerful animal.

We guide their whole bodies as well. Key words. “Guide” (metagomen, turn, direct). Control the mouth, control the horse.

Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds. Key words. Ancient merchant ships could be large; the ship that carried Paul held 276 people (Acts 27:37). Driven by fierce winds.

They are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs. Key words. “Rudder” (pēdaliou, steering oar). “Pilot” (euthynontos, the one steering). A small oar controls a great ship, even against strong winds.

What it does not mean. The illustrations do not mean the tongue is easy to control. They show its power: small, but it directs everything. The next verses show it is in fact hardest of all to control.

In a sentence. When we put bits into horses’ mouths to make them obey us, we can turn the whole animal. Or think of ships: although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wants to go.

On a Tuesday. Your tongue is steering your life and relationships. Where is it taking you? Ask God to take the rudder.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.

So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. Key words. “Member” (melos, part of the body). “Boasts of great things” (megala auchei, claims great power, brags). Small, but with enormous influence, for good or ill.

How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! Key words. “Forest” (hylēn, woodland, brushwood). “Small fire” (hēlikon pyr). A single spark can destroy a whole forest, as the dry hills of Palestine knew in summer. A single careless word can destroy a reputation, a friendship, a marriage, a church.

And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. Key words. “Fire” (pyr): destructive, spreading. “World of unrighteousness” (ho kosmos tēs adikias): the tongue contains in itself every kind of evil: lies, slander, gossip, flattery, boasting, cursing, false teaching. A whole world of sin in a small space.

The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body. Key words. “Set” (kathistatai, established, placed). “Staining” (spilousa, defiling, polluting), the opposite of “unstained” (1:27). What we say defiles our whole person (Matthew 15:11, 18).

Setting on fire the entire course of life. Key words. “Entire course of life” (ton trochon tēs geneseōs, the wheel of birth, the cycle of existence). An unusual phrase, perhaps borrowed from popular philosophy. The tongue sets the whole of life on fire, from beginning to end.

And set on fire by hell. Key words. “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final punishment (Matthew 5:22, 29–30; 10:28; 23:33; Mark 9:43–48). Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), later a symbol of God’s judgement. The destructive power of an evil tongue has its source in hell itself, in Satan, the father of lies (John 8:44).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the tongue can only do evil. It can bless, encourage, teach and pray (v. 9; Proverbs 12:18; 18:21). But uncontrolled, its potential for evil is immense. And “hell” does not mean the Valley of Hinnom was literally the place of final punishment; it became the name for the real, conscious, eternal punishment of the wicked.

In a sentence. In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it makes great boasts. Think how a whole forest is set on fire by a tiny spark. The tongue also is a fire, a world of evil among the parts of the body. It corrupts the whole person, sets the whole course of life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak, post or send a message this week, ask: will this light a fire? If so, don’t say it.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature. Key words. The four classes of animals from Genesis 1:26; 9:2. God gave humanity dominion over them.

Can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind. Key words. “Tamed” (damazetai, subdued, brought under control). Humans have tamed lions, elephants, falcons, snakes, even fish. Remarkable mastery over creation.

But no human being can tame the tongue. Key words. “No human being” (oudeis anthrōpōn, no one of mankind). We can tame wild beasts but not our own mouths. No human effort alone can bring the tongue under control. Only God can (Psalm 141:3; Proverbs 16:1).

It is a restless evil. Key words. “Restless” (akatastaton, unstable, unsettled), the same word as “unstable” (1:8). Like a wild animal pacing in a cage, never at rest, always ready to break out.

Full of deadly poison. Key words. “Deadly” (thanatēphorou, death-bringing). “Poison” (iou, venom), like a snake’s (Psalm 140:3; Romans 3:13). Words can kill: reputations, relationships, faith, and even lives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should give up trying to control our speech. What humans cannot do alone, God can do through his Spirit. Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).

In a sentence. Every kind of animal, bird, reptile and sea creature can be tamed and has been tamed by human beings, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

For worship. Pray Psalm 141:3 today: “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips!”

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

With it we bless our Lord and Father. Key words. “Bless” (eulogoumen, praise, speak well of). Jewish prayers often began, “Blessed are you, O Lord.” “Lord and Father”: the only place this combination appears in the New Testament.

And with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. Key words. “Curse” (katarōmetha, call down evil on, speak against). “Made in the likeness of God” (kath’ homoiōsin theou gegonotas, perfect tense: who have been made and remain in God’s likeness). From Genesis 1:26–27. Every human being bears God’s image, even after the fall (Genesis 9:6). To curse a person is to insult the God whose image they bear.

From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. Key words. The inconsistency: praising God on Sunday and slandering people on Monday; singing worship songs and then gossiping in the car park.

My brothers, these things ought not to be so. Key words. “Ought not” (ou chrē, it is not fitting, it must not be). A strong rebuke. This double-tongued behaviour is incompatible with genuine faith.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all strong language against evil. Jesus and the prophets denounced sin. It forbids cursing people, wishing them harm, and speaking with malice against those made in God’s image (Romans 12:14; Luke 6:28).

In a sentence. With the tongue we praise our Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in God’s likeness. Out of the same mouth come praise and cursing. My brothers and sisters, this should not be.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak about someone you dislike, remember: they bear God’s image. Speak of them as you would speak of God’s handiwork.

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.

Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Key words. “Spring” (pēgē, fountain). “Opening” (opēs, hole, crack). In dry Palestine, a good spring was precious. A spring gives one kind of water; it cannot give both sweet and bitter.

Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Key words. Nature is consistent: each plant produces according to its kind (Genesis 1:11–12). Jesus said the same: a tree is known by its fruit (Matthew 7:16–20; 12:33–35).

Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water. Key words. “Salt pond” (halykon, salt spring). The Dead Sea and salty springs near it could not produce drinkable water.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who sometimes speaks sinfully is not a believer. We all stumble (v. 2). It means the pattern of our speech reveals the nature of our heart (Luke 6:45). A heart renewed by God will increasingly produce good speech; persistent evil speech reveals an unrenewed heart.

In a sentence. Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? My brothers and sisters, can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.

For worship. Ask God to change the source: your heart. When he renews the spring, the water becomes sweet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James asks who among his readers is truly wise and understanding, and answers that wisdom proves itself in a good life lived with gentle humility. Where bitter envy and self-promotion fill the heart, boasting about wisdom is a lie against the truth. That kind of “wisdom” does not come from God; it is earthly, merely natural and even devilish, and it breeds disorder and every kind of wrong. God’s wisdom is marked first by purity, then by peace, gentleness, willingness to listen, mercy, good fruit, fairness and sincerity. Those who make peace sow seeds that grow into a harvest of righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

Wisdom is proved by good conduct in meekness. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, and almost every mark of it concerns how we treat others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition lay behind the quarrelling.

Now: The eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.

Who is wise and understanding among you? Key words. “Wise” (sophos): one who has practical, godly wisdom. “Understanding” (epistēmōn, knowledgeable, expert, skilful). Perhaps aimed at the would-be teachers (v. 1), who claimed wisdom.

By his good conduct let him show his works. Key words. “Show” (deixatō, demonstrate), as in 2:18. “Good conduct” (kalēs anastrophēs, beautiful way of life). Wisdom, like faith, is shown by works. Not by clever words or impressive knowledge, but by a beautiful life.

In the meekness of wisdom. Key words. “Meekness” (prautēti, gentleness, humility), as in 1:21. True wisdom is humble, gentle, not arrogant or aggressive. Moses was the meekest man on earth (Numbers 12:3); Jesus was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean wisdom is anti-intellectual. Understanding matters. But wisdom is measured by how we live, not by how much we know.

In a sentence. Who is wise and understanding among you? Let them show it by their good life, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.

On a Tuesday. Think of the wisest person you know. Is it their knowledge or their humble, good life that makes them wise? Aim for the same.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.

But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts. Key words. “Bitter” (pikron), like the salt water (v. 11). “Jealousy” (zēlon, zeal, but here in its bad sense, envy, rivalry). “Selfish ambition” (eritheian, self-seeking, party spirit; originally the word for politicians canvassing for office). Wanting to get ahead, be recognised, win.

Do not boast and be false to the truth. Key words. “Boast” (katakauchasthe, brag, exult over). “Be false to” (pseudesthe, lie against). Claiming to be wise while full of envy is a lie against the truth.

This is not the wisdom that comes down from above. Key words. True wisdom comes from God (1:5, 17). This is a counterfeit.

But is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. Key words. Three descending levels. “Earthly” (epigeios): belongs to this world, with its values. “Unspiritual” (psychikē, natural, soulish, belonging to the unregenerate human nature without the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 2:14; Jude 19). “Demonic” (daimoniōdēs, devilish, like demons): its ultimate source is the devil, whose original sin was pride and ambition.

For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice. Key words. “Disorder” (akatastasia, instability, confusion, unrest), related to “restless” (v. 8). “Vile” (phaulon, worthless, evil). Envy and ambition produce chaos in churches, families and workplaces, and open the door to every evil.

What it does not mean. It does not condemn all ambition. Wanting to serve God well and use our gifts fully is good (1 Corinthians 12:31; 1 Timothy 3:1). It condemns selfish ambition, which seeks one’s own glory at others’ expense.

In a sentence. But if you harbour bitter envy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast about it or deny the truth. Such “wisdom” does not come down from heaven, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where you have envy and selfish ambition, there you find disorder and every evil practice.

On a Tuesday. Is there envy or selfish ambition in your heart toward a colleague, a sibling, another believer? Confess it, and pray for their good.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

But the wisdom from above is first pure. Key words. “First” (prōton): above all, the foundation of the others. “Pure” (hagnē, holy, morally clean, without mixed motives). True wisdom begins with a pure heart before God.

Then peaceable. Key words. “Peaceable” (eirēnikē, peace-loving, seeking harmony). The opposite of the jealousy and disorder of verses 14–16. But peace comes after purity: never peace at the expense of truth or holiness.

Gentle. Key words. “Gentle” (epieikēs, gracious, considerate, forbearing, reasonable), as of elders (1 Timothy 3:3).

Open to reason. Key words. “Open to reason” (eupeithēs, easily persuaded, willing to yield, teachable, compliant). Not stubborn, but willing to listen and be corrected.

Full of mercy and good fruits. Key words. “Mercy” (eleous): compassion in action, as in 2:13. “Good fruits”: practical good deeds.

Impartial. Key words. “Impartial” (adiakritos, without wavering, undivided, unprejudiced). Both “not showing favouritism” (2:1–9) and “not double-minded” (1:6–8).

And sincere. Key words. “Sincere” (anypokritos, without hypocrisy, genuine, not play-acting).

And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. Key words. “Harvest” (karpos, fruit). “Sown” (speiretai). “Make peace” (poiousin eirēnēn). Peacemakers sow seeds of peace, which grow into a harvest of righteousness (Matthew 5:9; Hebrews 12:11). In contrast with envy, which produces disorder, peace produces righteousness. This list of qualities describes Jesus himself, who is wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30).

What it does not mean. “Peaceable” does not mean avoiding all conflict. Purity comes first; sometimes faithfulness requires confronting error. But the manner is gentle, reasonable and merciful.

In a sentence. But the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then it is peace-loving, considerate, willing to listen, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness.

For worship. Read the list slowly and see Jesus in each quality. Then ask God for this wisdom from above, as he has promised (1:5).

4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Chapter 4 goes to the root of the church’s failures. Quarrels come from desires at war within each person. Those desires come from friendship with the world, which is spiritual adultery against God. The remedy is humble submission: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, grieve over sin, humble yourselves. At the centre stands Proverbs 3:34: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” And “he gives more grace.”

The chapter ends with two warnings against taking God’s place: judging a brother, which sets us over the law, and planning as if tomorrow were ours, which forgets that we are a mist. The humble say, “If the Lord wills.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your fights come from desires at war inside you. You want and do not have, so you quarrel; you do not ask, or you ask to feed your desires. Friendship with the world is hostility to God. But God yearns jealously over us, and gives more grace: he opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. So submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands and hearts, grieve over sin, and humble yourselves, and he will lift you up.
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Quarrels come from desires at war within us, and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery. Yet God gives more grace — to the humble.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers prayed, but to fund the very desires that divided them.

Now: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near — and he will draw near to you.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Quarrels come from desires at war within us.

The war within. “Passions” is hēdonai, pleasures. The war is not first between factions but inside each person. Settle the presenting issue, and a person at war inside will find another.

“Murder”. Some have proposed reading “envy”, but the manuscripts do not support it. James is tracing sin to its root as Jesus did: hatred is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22). He is naming where desire is heading.

Desire, frustration, violence. The pattern twice. Thwarted desire is what sets the room on fire.

You do not ask. After all the heat, the simplest sentence. They organised life around getting, and never asked the God who gives generously (1:5).

On a Tuesday. Next time you are angry with your spouse or colleague, ask: what do I want that I am not getting? Then take that desire to God before you take it out on them.

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prayers fail when we ask to indulge our passions.

Praying to fund appetite. “Spend” is the word for the prodigal squandering his inheritance. These people are praying, but prayer has become a means of financing the desires that divide them.

Mercy in refusal. A father who funded every appetite would be negligent, not generous. God’s “no” here is kindness.

A searching question. When a prayer goes unanswered for years, ask not only “Why is God silent?” but also “What would I do with it if I got it?” This does not apply to genuine need, which James tells them to bring to God. It applies to desire.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friendship with the world is enmity with God.

Adulteresses. The Greek is feminine: the prophets’ language for Israel as an unfaithful bride (Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Quarrels and greed are not just bad behaviour; they are a marriage being broken.

The world. Not the planet or its people, whom God loves, but life organised without God.

No middle. Friendship with the world does not merely lead to enmity; it is enmity.

What it does not mean. Not that enjoying good things or living among unbelievers is sin. God gives every good gift (1:17). It is about where the heart’s affection points. The wishing is the adultery.

Makes himself. He has taken up a position. That is why grace can still reach him.
verseByVerse.note: The prophets called Israel’s unfaithfulness to God “adultery.”

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
God jealously desires the spirit he has placed in us, and gives more grace to the humble.

A hard verse. Verse 5 is difficult to translate, and no single Old Testament verse matches it; James seems to summarise a biblical theme. The ESV reading, that God yearns jealously over the spirit he gave us, fits the adultery of v. 4. Some read the spirit as the Holy Spirit, who yearns over us. Either way, God will not share us with the world.

Holy jealousy. Not pettiness, but a husband’s right response to a wife who is leaving. A God who felt nothing at our unfaithfulness would love us less, not more. Indifference is the opposite of love.

More grace. The turning point of the letter. Greater than the adultery, the quarrels, the appetite. Whatever sin has cost, the supply is larger.

Downhill. Grace flows down. “Opposes” is military: God lines up against the proud.

For worship. “But he gives more grace” is worth memorising. Say it whenever your sin seems bigger than God’s mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 5 is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers other readings. No single Old Testament verse matches it; it seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Submit to God, resist the devil, and draw near to God with clean hands and pure hearts.

Ten commands. Verses 7–10 hold ten imperatives, all unpacking “the humble”.

Submit first. A military word: arrange yourself under. Only then resist. A man who has not submitted to God has no standing from which to resist anything.

He will flee. Not a long siege. The devil cannot stand against a believer submitted to God.

How to resist. By standing firm in faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), putting on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:11–17), and answering lies with God’s word, as Jesus did (Matthew 4:1–11). Not by shouting at Satan or using formulas; even the archangel said only, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9).

Draw near. The priest’s word for approaching the altar. God is not waiting far off; he already yearns over us. Think of the father who ran (Luke 15:20).

Hands and hearts. Outward conduct and inward loyalty. And “double-minded” at last receives its remedy: purification, after “he gives more grace”.

On a Tuesday. When a familiar temptation comes, do three things: submit (“Lord, I am yours”), resist (say no, and quote a verse), draw near (pray for a minute). The order matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentance mourns over sin, and God exalts the humble.

A call to repentance. The letter began, “Count it all joy”. So why gloom? Because these people were quarrelling and coveting cheerfully. The laughter to be turned to mourning is the laughter of people not taking their sin seriously.

What it does not mean. Not permanent gloom or misery as a spiritual state. It is godly grief, which “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10), and leads to joy.

Who does what. The humbling is ours; the lifting is God’s. That is the reverse of our default, where we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us. It is the pattern of Christ (Philippians 2:8–9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not slander one another. Judging a brother sets you over the law instead of under it; there is one Lawgiver and Judge. And do not plan as though tomorrow were yours. You are a mist. Say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Boasting about the future is evil, and whoever knows the right thing to do and does not do it, sins.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Speaking against a brother sets us over the law instead of under it. And whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The merchants' plan was complete except for God.

Now: Plan, but hold every plan under “if the Lord wills” — life itself included.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speaking evil of a brother puts oneself above the law and its one Lawgiver and Judge.

Speak against. From slander to the accurate but damaging remark: the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the church.

Judging the law. The law says love your neighbour (2:8). Condemning him sets that law aside, ruling it does not apply here. A judge stands over the law; a doer stands under it.

One Judge. Only one can act on the verdict either way.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never judge. We test teaching (1 John 4:1), and the church exercises discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What is forbidden is slander, and condemning a brother as if we were his final judge.

Neighbour. The last word brings back Leviticus 19:18. The person you are judging is the one you were commanded to love.

On a Tuesday. In a conversation about an absent church member, ask yourself: would I say this to his face, in love? If not, change the subject, or pray for him instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plans for business and profit must acknowledge that life is a mist and depends on the Lord’s will.

A complete plan. Timing, destination, duration, activity, outcome. Nothing wrong with any of it. Trade, profit and planning are not condemned (Proverbs 6:6–8).

What is missing. One clause. The plan assumes knowledge no one has.

A mist. The haze over a field that is gone when the sun is up: not a short life, but a brief appearance.

If the Lord wills. James does not cancel the trip. He adds the clause, and it covers living as well as doing.

What it does not mean. Not a formula to tack onto sentences. One person can say the words with no real dependence; another can plan the whole year in that spirit without saying them once.

On a Tuesday. As you put next year’s holiday in the diary, pause and pray: “Lord, if you will, we will live and go.” David’s prayer is ours: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boasting in plans is evil, and knowing the right thing and not doing it is sin.

Arrogance. The word first described a travelling quack claiming powers he did not have.

Evil. Not naive but evil: a mist claiming the knowledge and control that belong to God.

Sin as omission. “So” ties v. 17 to the passage: now they know about the mist and “if the Lord wills”. Sin is not only doing what is forbidden, but not doing what is known to be right.

The whole letter in one sentence. The hearer who does not do (1:22), the speaker who does not give (2:16), the one who knows and does not act. James never charges them with ignorance, but with being informed.

On a Tuesday. Every sermon understood and every book agreed with raises the stakes. Pick one thing you already know you should do, and do it today.
